facts.text: Farmington Hills became a city in 1973, when the remainder of Farmington Township and the villages of Quakertown and Wood Creek Farms were incorporated together.

Farmington and Farmington Hills are separate cities with their own services and addresses, but they are often thought of as one community and share Farmington Public Schools and the Farmington Community Library.
Major thoroughfares in Farmington Hills include M-5, Orchard Lake Road, 12 Mile Road, 8 Mile Road, Northwestern Highway, I-696 and I-275.
Wood Creek Farms was developed as a subdivision in 1937 and incorporated as a village in 1957 before becoming part of Farmington Hills in 1973.
The City of Farmington Hills holds an annual holiday lights celebration at City Hall, at the corner of Eleven Mile and Orchard Lake roads; the 2025 celebration, the 33rd, was held on December 2.
Heritage Park, a 211-acre park on the west side of Farmington Road between Ten and Eleven Mile roads, has 4.5 miles of trails, the city's Nature Center and the Spicer House.
The historic Longacre House on Farmington Road is a banquet and event facility with a running stone wall fence and gardens.
Harrison High School closed in 2019, and its building was repurposed as The Hawk, the city's community center.
The city's Historic District Commission works to establish and preserve local historic districts and publishes a Historic Structures Map of Farmington Hills.

christmas-light-installation.title: Christmas Light Installation in Farmington Hills, MI
christmas-light-installation.meta_description: Christmas light installation in Farmington Hills, MI for 1930s homes and newer subdivisions alike, hung by bucket-truck crews and removed after the season.
christmas-light-installation.h1: Christmas Light Installation in Farmington Hills, MI
christmas-light-installation.hero_sub: Homes here span nearly a century of building. We design lighting that suits your home's age and shape, install it with bucket-truck crews and remove it after the holidays.
christmas-light-installation.local_paragraph: Farmington Hills is a patchwork of eras. Wood Creek Farms was laid out as a subdivision in 1937, the old village of Quakertown became part of the new city in 1973, and newer neighborhoods filled in around them. That range shows up across the city, so no single plan fits every house. We design each home on its own terms, placing lights where they flatter the architecture, wrapping the trees worth featuring and keeping the whole design balanced. Our crews then hang it, keep it shining through the season and remove it when the holidays wrap up.
considerations: Neighborhoods that date back to the 1930s often have trees that tower over the house. Wrapping the trunk and main limbs of one or two can anchor a whole display, and bucket trucks make the height manageable. We suggest which trees frame the home best, and you decide which ones make the final plan.
Matching the design to the era

A 1930s home and a newer multi-peak house call for different plans. Older houses tend to look right with a single warm roofline and lit shrubs by the entry, while larger modern rooflines can carry more runs and wrapped trees without looking busy.

The city holds an annual holiday lights celebration at City Hall, at Eleven Mile and Orchard Lake, and the 2025 event fell on December 2. To have the house lit in time, put your request in well ahead. Installs usually land between October and early December, and earlier requests have more dates to choose from.
faq: Does your service area include Farmington too?

Yes. The two are separate cities, but both are in Oakland County and inside our Southeast Michigan service area. They share schools and a library and are often thought of as one community, and we treat them the same way: the same full service in either city, starting with a free estimate.
What if my home is on the Historic Structures Map?

We can plan for it. Check with the city's Historic District Commission about what applies to your property first. Seasonal lights attach temporarily, and we keep fastening to places that suit older materials. The design plan helps if the city asks what you intend.
What happens after I request an estimate?

We reach out to talk through what you have in mind and look at the home, then send a free estimate. That estimate spans the whole season, from design and installation to service calls and removal, and it lists exactly what is included.

commercial-holiday-lighting.title: Commercial Holiday Lighting in Farmington Hills, MI
commercial-holiday-lighting.meta_description: Offices, retail centers, HOAs and managed properties in Farmington Hills, MI get holiday lighting built for busy corridors. Design, install, takedown.
commercial-holiday-lighting.h1: Commercial Holiday Lighting in Farmington Hills, MI
commercial-holiday-lighting.hero_sub: Office buildings, retail centers, association entrances and managed properties, lit in clean lines that read from Northwestern Highway, 12 Mile or Orchard Lake Road.
commercial-holiday-lighting.local_paragraph: Farmington Hills is a city of corridors. M-5, Orchard Lake Road, 12 Mile, 8 Mile, Northwestern Highway, I-696 and I-275 are its major thoroughfares, and the businesses along them are mostly seen from the driver's seat. Holiday lighting for an office building or retail center here should be bold and clean: an outlined roofline, lit entrance trees and pole decor that marks the driveway from a distance. For HOAs and property managers, entrance displays and common-area trees give residents a warm arrival every evening. Your property gets its own design, then bucket-truck installation, service while it is up and removal once the holidays are done.
considerations: Office properties are seen at both ends of a December workday, when it is often dark on arrival and dark again at departure. A crisp building outline and lit entry trees make both moments warmer and keep the site looking cared for after hours.

Large parking areas make pole and lamppost decor worth considering. Wrapped or decorated poles mark the path from the road to the front door and extend the display across the property without crowding the building itself.

In a condo community, the shared spaces carry the holidays for everyone. We light entrance signs, clubhouse rooflines and common-area trees, and the estimate itemizes each piece so the board can approve a clear, complete scope.
faq: What do you light for offices in Farmington Hills?

Building outlines, entry trees, pole decor and entrance signs are the usual starting points. We light offices and business campuses, as well as retail centers, HOAs and managed properties, and Farmington Hills sits inside our service area. The free estimate starts with the address and a look at the property with your facilities contact.
How do installs fit around our business hours?

We set the schedule with your facilities team before the crew arrives. Tell us about delivery windows, busy entrances or tenant rules, and the install will be planned around them. High runs go up from bucket trucks, which keeps ladders out of the doorways people use most.
Can the display include our landscaping and signage?

Yes. Beyond the building, we light trees and shrubs, entrance signs, poles and lampposts, and bistro string lighting for patios or courtyards. We also offer landscape lighting for year-round use. Each element appears on the estimate, so you can adjust the scope.

permanent-lighting.title: Permanent Roofline Lighting in Farmington Hills, MI
permanent-lighting.meta_description: Farmington Hills permanent roofline lighting, controlled from an app: an everyday accent most nights and holiday colors in December. Free estimate.
permanent-lighting.h1: Permanent Lighting in Farmington Hills, MI
permanent-lighting.hero_sub: A roofline that is ready for every season, planned around your home's age and trim, then run from an app so the ladder stays in the garage.
permanent-lighting.local_paragraph: Farmington Hills homes range from 1930s neighborhoods to newer subdivisions, and permanent lighting can suit many of them once the roofline is planned well. Mounted once along the eaves, the lights stay up all year and answer to an app. In December they can glow warm white or full color for the holidays, and on a fall Saturday they can take on a team's colors. On an ordinary weeknight, a soft white line along the roof is often all a house needs. The lights stay in place between seasons, so the design has to look right in July as well as in December.
considerations: On an older house, mounting points are chosen to suit the original trim and fascia, and the runs follow the lines that define the home. Newer houses with long eaves are simpler, but they still get a layout planned run by run before anything is attached.

A permanent roofline does not need a spot on the fall install calendar each year. Once it is up, the house is ready for the city's holiday lights celebration at City Hall and every holiday after it, with nothing more than a change in the app.

Permanent lighting does not have to wrap the whole house on day one. The front roofline and garage face the street and carry most of the effect, and other sections can be added later. The estimate shows exactly which runs are included.
faq: Does permanent lighting cover Farmington too, or only Farmington Hills?

Both. The two cities are separate, with their own addresses and services, but both sit inside our service area. During the free estimate we review your eaves and peaks and the seasons you care about most, then detail the scope so you know exactly what is included.
Do I need approval for permanent lighting on an older home?

It depends on the property. The city's Historic District Commission works to preserve local historic districts and publishes a Historic Structures Map, so check with the city if your home may be affected. If your neighborhood has an association, check its guidelines too.
Do you also offer landscape lighting?

Yes. Landscape lighting for paths, trees and the front of the home is one of our services, and it pairs naturally with a permanent roofline. One estimate can cover both, with the layout and what is included spelled out.
